headline: Vinva has partnered with Magellan for Australian retail distribution, allowing Vinva to remain focused solely on investment performance
reasoning: Waked explains that the Magellan partnership is specifically about accessing Magellan's established national retail distribution network in Australia. Vinva brings the investment product and performance focus while Magellan handles distribution, allowing Vinva to avoid building its own distribution team. This keeps Vinva's attention on investment outcomes rather than commercial infrastructure.
quote: So the, the partnership with Magellan is really around distribution and predominantly around Australian retail distribution. You know, as I said before, our focus is really on investment performance. Um, we want to bring our style of investing to the retail market and our skill and our focus not on building out a distribution team. Um, so the partnership with Magellan is they've got good national distribution, a high quality team. Uh, we've got the investment product, um, and that can distribute our products into the retail market.
episode_title: Morry Waked and the rise of an investing juggernaut

headline: Morry Waked reflects on early days of quantitative investing in Australia and the opportunity to bring scientific discipline to equity markets
reasoning: Morry Waked describes joining Rothschild's quantitative research team in the early-to-mid 1990s, at a time when quant investing was in its infancy in Australia. He notes Rothschild was an early mover in systematic/quantitative approaches alongside a fundamental active management tradition. He saw an opportunity to apply mathematical rigour and modelling to support the investment team's decision-making, which he recognised as a meaningful gap in the market. This background formed the foundation for what eventually became Vinva Investment Management.
quote: A couple of years or so into it, I started to realize that there's great opportunity here. You know, at the end of the day, what we're trying to do is as a firm back then is trying to get sort... Rothschild was a bit of an early mover in that space. So I think they saw me as a good young kid and the guys I worked with it, being able to provide them with some support, you know, build some sort of data for them, do some charts, you know, do some sort of simple modeling that could sort of help them in their decision making.
episode_title: Morry Waked and the rise of an investing juggernaut

headline: Vinva sees active global equities as the primary long-term growth engine, with capacity to double or triple AUM over 20 years
reasoning: Morry Waked identifies active global equities as Vinva's core growth driver, noting that global markets are larger, more liquid and deeper than the Australian market. He believes Vinva could manage double or triple its current ~$47.5bn AUM over the next 20 years. The firm is focused on winning global institutional clients rather than building out its own distribution infrastructure.
quote: So our ability, if I look at the business, uh, you know, down the track, yeah, we could be managing double, potentially triple what we're managing in 20 years time, um, because the real growth engine of our businesses is active global equities, uh, and those marks are much bigger, more liquid, more deeper than the Australian market.
episode_title: Morry Waked and the rise of an investing juggernaut

headline: Vinva's Morry Waked reflects on the evolution and growth of systematic/quantitative investing in Australian equities from the late 1990s onwards
reasoning: Waked describes how he developed a systematic, quantitative investment approach at Barclays Global Investors (BGI) in Australia starting in 1997, beginning with $100 million in Australian equities. The approach focused on fundamental data, valuation metrics, and changes in investor expectations rather than traditional analyst coverage. The strategy delivered consistent moderate outperformance, growing from $100M to $26 billion AUM in Australian equities alone by 2004-05. Waked emphasises that while computers provided scalability and efficiency, investment professionals remained at the core of decision-making. He notes that 'garbage in, garbage out' — investment sensibility must underpin quantitative inputs.
quote: One of the things I learned early on is, you know, fortunate at BGI, I was, I was fortunate enough to stand on the shoulders of giants. Some wonderful intellectual leaders and thought leaders in this space globally and pioneers. So I was fortunate enough to work with them and really stand on their shoulders. And one of the things you learn ultimately is that everything has to start with the investment sensibility. We're investment professionals first, we're quantitative professionals second, if I could put it that way. So like any good active manager, you know, the inputs that went into our process, you know, a lot of around fundamentals, you know, looking at sort of a range of different sort of metrics.
episode_title: Morry Waked and the rise of an investing juggernaut

headline: Vinva emphasises forward-looking assumptions over backward-looking data, tilting toward less-crowded and less-obvious market signals
reasoning: Morry Waked articulates that the firm's edge lies not in rear-view-mirror analysis of historical data but in making forward-looking assumptions about where markets are heading. He stresses the importance of understanding market dynamics, identifying where trades are crowded or obvious, and tilting toward less obvious opportunities. The firm also tracks what data is more or less important, and continuously evolves its models — much of what was used in 2010 has since been replaced. Humility and awareness of the limits of one's knowledge are presented as critical traits for sustained active management outperformance.
quote: Our approach is not looking through the rear view mirror and looking at what worked in the past... our job as investment professionals is to look through the windscreen and make assumptions about where things are heading. And that's where it's important to understand market dynamics, where things may be crowded, where things are more obvious and tilt the things that are less obvious, that's where the people, um, skills and insights come into play. And what data we think is more important. What data do we think is less important? To be successful in active management and to be successful consistently over a long period of time, you need a good dose of modesty and humility because markets can be very humbling.
episode_title: Morry Waked and the rise of an investing juggernaut

headline: Vinva shifted to global-to-local modelling framework, recognising interconnected capital markets over siloed geographic analysis
reasoning: Morry Waked describes a major intellectual evolution at Vinva roughly 15 years ago, when the firm moved away from using purely local market data to forecast local stock returns. The insight was that companies do not operate in isolation — around a third of Australian companies' revenues and assets are derived offshore, and US tech companies sell into Asia and source components from Asia. This led Vinva to treat global markets as a single integrated capital market rather than 40–50 separate ones. The firm then built models incorporating customer-supplier relationships across geographies, which they call 'global to local' modelling.
quote: A lot of the research and a lot of the models that we'd built, you know, pre-2009 say, we're very much using local information in each of the markets around the world and using that local data to forecast local stock returns and the relative is around them. And you start thinking in a bigger picture and breaking down geographic boundaries and you think, well, you know, a lot of these companies that don't operate in isolation in their own markets or in their own industries, they're connected to many other companies around the world. A third of Australian companies, revenues and assets are derived from offshore. You look at those US tech companies, you know, they're not just selling to people in the US, they're selling to people in Asia and they're buying, you know, chips and other sorts of things from Asia. So you start looking at it as one big global capital market, rather than 40 or 50 markets, then you say, okay, let's look at customer supply relationships, like any good investment analysis would probably think of. So we started developing models that were more what we call global to local.
episode_title: Morry Waked and the rise of an investing juggernaut
